extra.message: String comparison via '!=' operator at line 118 (verifier != known[handle]) is not constant-time. An attacker can use timing side-channels to successively determine correct verifier values, effectively forging authentication for the protected operations. The application should use hmac.compare_digest() instead.

At line 125-128, the request's Origin header is read and directly reflected into the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header with credentials allowed. An attacker controlling any external site can make cross-origin requests to this endpoint with the victim's browser, and arbitrary origins are echoed back. This effectively creates a wildcard CORS policy.

At line 135, X-XSS-Protection header is set to '0' (disabling the browser XSS filter), and at line 136, Content-Security-Policy is set to an empty string. These disable all recommended browser-side security headers, making the response more susceptible to XSS and other client-side attacks.

At line 176, access to elevated privileges (payroll full access, casework open) is granted based on checking that a cookie or header value equals 'lead'. An attacker can simply set the 'ops_badge' cookie or 'x-ops-badge' header to 'lead' from any client to gain elevated access without authorization. The authorization is trivially bypassable.

At line 42, the authorization header from request.headers.get('authorization') is logged via logger.warning(). If an attacker sends a Bearer token or other credentials, they will be permanently stored in the application logs, risking credential exposure to anyone with log access.

extra.message: The Django SECRET_KEY defaults to the hardcoded string 'dev-only-change-me' (line 8) when DJANGO_SECRET_KEY environment variable is not set. This is a well-known default that any attacker can predict, allowing them to forge Django sessions, CSRF tokens, and cryptographic signatures.

The default database URL at line 53 is hardcoded as 'postgres://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/generated_hr_payroll_django' with default postgres credentials. If DATABASE_URL is not set, the application will connect with these default credentials, which are easily guessable by attackers who obtain the source code.

At line 26-27, when DEBUG is True (which is the default per settings.py line 9), media files are served directly via Django's development file viewer. If DEBUG is accidentally left on in production, this causes the media directory to be publicly accessible and exposes PII/financial documents.

DEMO_PASSWORD is hardcoded as 'DemoPass123!' at line 27 and applied to all demo user accounts (line 47). If this code is deployed to non-demo environments, all users share the same easily-guessable password, completely defeating authentication. The password is also printed to stdout at line 107.

At line 465, all imported employees are assigned the hardcoded password 'ChangeMe123!' via set_password(). Any imported user can immediately log in with this trivially guessable password before they are forced to change it.

At line 27, getattr(user, 'employee_profile', None) could return None if the authenticated user has no EmployeeProfile (which is allowed by the model — the FK is not nullable, but role_for() already guards for None). If user has no profile, line 29 attempts .id on None when checking manager_id, potentially causing an AttributeError that leaks stack traces. Similarly at line 28, the expression evaluates 'or' on a None check followed by a .id access.

At line 161-162, cryptographic nonces are generated using random.choice() with a default alphabet string, which uses Python's insecure Mersenne Twister PRNG. An attacker who observes a small number of generated codes can predict future codes and impersonate other users.
